description: The Soviet economy in 1949 as the same seven industries, valued at 1949 US prices (as the CIA valued Soviet output). Heavy industry and farming dominate; light industry and services are starved. Reconciled so the 1949 accounts close exactly. A first estimate built from Western reconstructions, not from Soviet input–output tables (the first was published for 1959).

sources.label: Abram Bergson, The Real National Income of Soviet Russia since 1928 (1961)
Richard Moorsteen and Raymond Powell, The Soviet Capital Stock, 1928–1962 (1966)
CIA, dollar valuations of Soviet GNP (declassified series)
Maddison Project Database (relative size of the Soviet economy)

valueAddedShare.note: Share of business value added. Collective and state farms employed about half the Soviet labour force in 1950.

valueAddedRatio.note: Soviet farming bought fewer inputs per rouble of output than American farming: little fertiliser, few tractors.

inputs.note: Seed and feed from farms, machinery and repairs from the machine–tractor stations (heavy industry), fuel, fertiliser, and haulage.

imports.note: Imports of farm products, 1949, $bn at US prices: wool, hides, rubber and tropical produce, mostly from the bloc and China.

capitalShare.note: Share of fixed capital: farm buildings, livestock, tractors.

valueAddedShare.note: Share of business value added: coal and ore mining, metallurgy, machine-building, construction and armaments. Stalin's 'Group A'.

valueAddedRatio.note: Soviet heavy industry was notoriously material-intensive: more metal and fuel per rouble of output than in the West.

inputs.note: Mostly its own products (ore, coal, metal, machines), plus rail freight, timber, fuel and chemicals.

imports.note: Imports of machinery and metals, 1949, $bn: much of it from East Germany and Czechoslovakia, including reparations.

capitalShare.note: Share of fixed capital: mines, steelworks, machine plants.

investmentShare.note: Share of 1949 investment: the post-war reconstruction of the Donbass and the Urals.

valueAddedShare.note: Share of business value added: oil, gas and electricity (coal is in heavy industry).

valueAddedRatio.note: Value added per dollar of output.

inputs.note: Coal for power stations, equipment, crude oil to refineries, rail and pipeline transport.

imports.note: Imports of fuel from Romania and elsewhere in the bloc, 1949, $bn.

capitalShare.note: Share of fixed capital: power stations, oilfields, refineries.

valueAddedShare.note: Share of business value added: food processing, textiles, clothing and footwear. Stalin's 'Group B'.

valueAddedRatio.note: Mostly farm materials processed, so value added per dollar is low.

inputs.note: Grain, meat, cotton and flax from farms; its own intermediate goods; fuel, freight and some metal.

imports.note: Imports of textiles and processed goods from the bloc, 1949, $bn.

capitalShare.note: Share of fixed capital: mills and food plants.

investmentShare.note: Share of 1949 investment: light industry was starved of investment.

valueAddedShare.note: Share of business value added: chemicals, electrical engineering, aviation, instruments and communications.

valueAddedRatio.note: Value added per dollar of output.

inputs.note: Metals and machinery, its own components, fuel, freight and services.

investmentShare.note: Share of 1949 investment, including the atomic and aviation programmes.

valueAddedShare.note: Share of business value added: housing, personal services and finance. Health and education are government in the USSR and sit in its workforce.

valueAddedRatio.note: Mostly labour and the (low, state-set) rental value of housing.

inputs.note: Building repairs, fuel and power, supplies, and other services.

capitalShare.note: Share of fixed capital, mostly housing: less than in the West because Soviet cities were chronically overcrowded.

investmentShare.note: Share of 1949 investment: rebuilding war-destroyed housing.

valueAddedShare.note: Share of business value added: the railways (the backbone of Soviet freight), river and sea transport, and state and cooperative trade.

valueAddedRatio.note: Value added per dollar of output.

inputs.note: Coal and fuel, rolling stock and repairs, packaging and services.

capitalShare.note: Share of fixed capital: railways above all.

capitalOutputRatio.note: Fixed capital divided by GNP, 1949. The war destroyed about a quarter of the pre-war stock (Moorsteen and Powell), leaving capital scarce relative to labour; that scarcity is why returns to post-war investment, and growth, were so high.

depreciation.note: Soviet retirement rates were low: plant was kept running long past its Western lifetime.

fixed_investment.note: What Soviet investment bought: construction and machinery above all, some electrical equipment and freight.

inventory_investment.note: Which products are stocked or run down.

state_local.note: Civil government in the USSR: administration, health, education and science. Over half is pay for doctors, teachers, officials and scientists.

exports.note: Soviet exports: grain and timber, ores, metals, coal and machinery for the bloc, oil, furs and textiles.

aid_exports.note: Aid shipments abroad, if any: grain, machinery and fuel.

defence.note: Soviet defence: conscripts were paid little, so pay is a smaller share than in America; tanks, artillery, ammunition and fortifications (heavy industry), aircraft, radar and the atomic programme (technology), food and uniforms.

research.note: Academy of Sciences institutes and design bureaux.

physicalIndicators.note: Steel tonnage moves with heavy industry's real output.
